name: Macadamia nuts
summary: Macadamia nuts are rich, buttery nuts from a tree native to Australia, eaten raw, roasted or salted. This page lists what people say macadamia nuts do; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Macadamia nuts are high in fat, mostly monounsaturated: the main fat is oleic acid, with a lot of palmitoleic acid too. A 2004 study found it in macadamia oil, and also tocopherols, squalene and plant sterols.

The UK food table (CoFID) has only a salted entry, at 748 kcal, 77.6 g of fat (11.2 g of it saturated), 7.9 g of protein, 4.0 g of sugars, 100 mg of magnesium and 0.28 mg of thiamin per 100 g, with 400 mg of sodium from the salt. It does not measure fibre for this entry, nor tocopherols, squalene or plant sterols.
processing: The table's macadamia entry is salted, so its 400 mg of sodium per 100 g comes from added salt; plain nuts hold less, and this page has no measured figure for them.

whoShouldBeCareful.note: A 2015 systematic review says tree nuts are among the most common foods causing acute allergic reactions and that nearly all tree nuts have been linked to fatal reactions. If you react to nuts, talk to your doctor or an allergist.

unknowns: Whether eating macadamia nuts changes long-term health outcomes: the trials found lower LDL cholesterol compared with an average American diet over five weeks in 25 people with slightly raised cholesterol, which says little about years.
What the table's salted entry says about plain macadamia nuts: only the salted entry is in the table.
Whether people in Greece or Rome knew macadamias: they did not, and this page found no older written source that could be opened and read.
